poster.title: The Metamorphosis
poster.bookOrigin: German-language Prague literature by Franz Kafka; historical Bohemia, present-day Czechia. The displayed wrapper was published in Leipzig.
poster.creator: Ottomar Starke
poster.alt: An ochre wrapper with red German title lettering above a dark illustration of a person covering his face beside an open door; small publisher and 1916 lines below.
poster.blurb: A covered face and an open doorway leave the central event unseen.

notes.title: The displayed edition
notes.body: Leipzig: Kurt Wolff Verlag, catalogued 1916 by the Leo Baeck Institute. The visible wrapper says 1916; the story appeared in 1915. This copy is not labelled a 1915 first printing.

notes.title: Writing and image-making
notes.body: The institutional record credits Ottomar Starke’s illustrated wrapper for Kafka’s work. The pictured gesture and doorway are described without identifying an undocumented narrative moment.

notes.title: A visible design relationship
notes.body: Red lettering establishes the title above the dense black doorway. The figure bends while the frame remains rigid and upright.

studyData.intro: An open door, a covered face and a red title show an event indirectly. This study examines the wrapper catalogued as 1916, keeping that object separate from the story’s 1915 publication.

regions.label: A face hidden by hands
regions.summary: The figure bends forward with both hands raised over the face.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The figure bends forward with both hands raised over the face. Dark clothing joins into a single curved mass beside the straighter doorway.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The gesture can suggest distress or withdrawal without showing what the figure sees. It creates an emotional point of entry while leaving the cause outside the image.

regions.question: What can a hidden face communicate that an explicit expression might not?

regions.label: An opening that conceals
regions.summary: A dark door leaf projects forward from the frame.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A dark door leaf projects forward from the frame. Its near edge is a strong vertical and its lower edge angles towards the floor.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The opening directs attention towards a space that remains obscure. The cover makes a threshold legible while withholding a clear view of what lies beyond it.

regions.question: Does the dark opening feel like an invitation, a barrier or something else?

regions.label: Rectangles within the doorway
regions.summary: Nested upright rectangles divide the visible door and frame.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Nested upright rectangles divide the visible door and frame. They stand close to the rounded shoulder and bent arm of the figure.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Regular panels can make the figure’s bodily tension more apparent. The comparison depends on the contrast of shapes rather than a literal account of the scene.

regions.question: How do the straight panels alter your reading of the bent body?

regions.label: Hatching gives the room weight
regions.summary: Short overlapping dark strokes spread across the floor beneath the shoes and doorway.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Short overlapping dark strokes spread across the floor beneath the shoes and doorway. Their density changes across the ochre paper.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The hatching supplies a shared ground for figure and architecture. It prevents the separate shapes from appearing as unrelated symbols floating on the wrapper.

regions.question: Which floor marks most strongly connect the figure to the door?

regions.label: A warm line above the dark picture
regions.summary: Die Verwandlung is printed in red across most of the width.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Die Verwandlung is printed in red across most of the width. The line sits above the black illustration with a small interval of plain paper.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The colour change makes the title a separate reading event. Its broad horizontal line briefly steadies an image dominated by inward movement and darkness.

sections.heading: A title about change
sections.body: Die Verwandlung names a transformation. The established English title The Metamorphosis is given here to connect the German wording to the familiar work, without changing the cover’s own text.

regions.question: Would a black title feel as distinct from the hatchings below?

regions.label: A quiet name at the top
regions.summary: Franz Kafka appears in small spaced capitals above the title.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Franz Kafka appears in small spaced capitals above the title. The name occupies less width and has more paper around it than the red line below.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The hierarchy gives the work’s title greater visual force than its author. A familiar name can still be found easily because its isolated position is clear.

sections.heading: Prague writing, Leipzig publishing
sections.body: Kafka belonged to Prague’s German-language literary world. The museum chronology records the story’s publication in 1915, while the Leo Baeck Institute catalogues this Leipzig wrapper as 1916. The work’s literary context and the pictured edition’s place are therefore recorded separately.

regions.question: What does the space around the small author line contribute to its visibility?

regions.label: A series named beneath the scene
regions.summary: Der jüngste Tag and the numbers 22/23 sit between thin horizontal rules beneath the illustration.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Der jüngste Tag and the numbers 22/23 sit between thin horizontal rules beneath the illustration. The lettering is compact and widely spaced.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The ruled line changes the mode from dramatic picture to publishing information. It offers a more ordered footer after the irregular hatchings above.

regions.question: How do the thin rules tell you that this line has a different role?

regions.label: A date attached to this object
regions.summary: The small digits 1916 sit below the publisher and Leipzig line.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The small digits 1916 sit below the publisher and Leipzig line. Their wide spacing makes a short date into a modest centred unit.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: A visible date can help identify a physical edition, but it need not be the year the work first appeared. Keeping these roles separate changes how a chronology is read.

sections.heading: The catalogued wrapper
sections.body: The Leo Baeck Institute identifies Kurt Wolff Verlag in Leipzig, dates the object 1916, and credits Ottomar Starke’s illustration. This study uses that selected object date rather than silently converting it into a 1915 first-edition claim.

regions.question: Which date would you use for the story, and which for this wrapper?

regions.label: Ochre space around the drawing
regions.summary: Warm ochre paper surrounds the image and the fine imprint.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Warm ochre paper surrounds the image and the fine imprint. Uneven tone, faint creases and worn edges remain visible in the reproduction.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Material ageing changes the present colour relationship. The wrapper can be studied as it survives without treating this screen colour as an original ink specification.

regions.question: How might fresh paper have changed the contrast of the red and black marks?

regions.label: Body and architecture meet
regions.summary: The figure’s lower clothing, shoes and angled door edge approach the same patch of hatched floor.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The figure’s lower clothing, shoes and angled door edge approach the same patch of hatched floor. Several directions meet in a small area.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: This junction makes the threshold spatial rather than merely symbolic. It is also where the body’s diagonal movement most clearly meets the rigid room.

regions.question: Where does your eye move when the clothing, floor and door edges converge?

connections.label: An uneasy threshold
connections.title: A gesture beside an opening
connections.text: The covered face turns inward beside the door’s outward opening.

connections.label: Different emphasis
connections.title: Red words, black picture
connections.text: The title’s red line is quickly readable above the dense black architectural hatchings.
